<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases, but B's answers to the two most important structural pressures held up better. On funding, A's central claim that a ban "forecloses forever" any recapture mechanism was met with the ordinary and plausible counter that broad legalization grows the tax base itself (more taxed doors over years), which A never fully dismantled beyond reasserting the dilemma. On production/pace, B's "fifty lots vs. fifty thousand lots" argument — that if labor/materials are the real constraint, maximizing eligible parcels yields more total output than gating a small pool behind lottery/owner-occupancy/parking conditions — directly attacked A's repeated "same pace either way" premise, and A's reply (friction is "minor" so it's costless either way) didn't fully answer the eligibility-pool logic. B also raised an equity point (wealthy areas keep exclusion while poor corridors absorb density under calibrated regimes) that A never addressed. A's strongest contributions — the durability-via-vested-permits argument and the "screw-tightening cuts both ways" rebuttal — were solid but were met with a scale asymmetry response from B (thousands of dispersed owners vs. a few dozen bonus-gated lots) that was never squarely neutralized. The debate was close and both closings crystallized the clash well, but B left fewer live, unanswered threats hanging over its case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's "fifty lots vs. fifty thousand lots" rebuttal in R1/R2, which used A's own concession that construction pace is labor-limited to argue that broader eligibility (not narrower, gated bonus programs) maximizes output with the same labor pool — a point A never fully answered beyond calling the friction "minor."</best_rebuttal>
